title: LMFAO
intro: LMFAO turns refusing an argument into a way of winning it. The speaker calls conflict childish, dismisses the other person's hurt and then enjoys a prolonged playground taunt. For most of the song, crying belongs to the opponent and laughter to him. The ending puts both responses inside one expression of exasperation, loosening that clean division. The performance's pleasure lies in the contradiction: he will not engage, but he wants the other person to hear exactly how triumphantly he is not engaging.
reading: Refusal becomes participation; the ending collapses the assigned winner/loser emotional roles.

revisions.editorial-27-childish: Calling the dispute childish gives him the position of the mature person who can decline it. But 'keep crying' later uses the very playground cruelty he claims to have outgrown. That mismatch is the song's engine, not a detail to smooth away. The refusal is itself an aggressive contribution to the argument: he withholds recognition while ensuring that the other person knows they have been dismissed.
revisions.editorial-27-mock-apology: The apology presents another person's disappointment as an accidental consequence of his enormous ambition. Yet he has just said he cannot let them get their way. The supposed accident is therefore also something he actively wants. Politeness lets him deny responsibility for a humiliation he is staging, which makes the voice more pointed than a simple statement of confidence.
revisions.27-n3: The closing expression means being unable to laugh or cry appropriately at an absurd or frustrating situation. Before it arrives, the song assigns the two reactions to separate people, then reduces them to alternating single words. Joining them finally disrupts the neat emotional scoreboard. It does not prove that he secretly cries; it makes the ending less securely triumphant than the preceding 'you cry, I laugh' routine.
